fit: perioperative ginger and distinct nausea, vomiting and rescue outcomes
assessment: The review reports inconclusive postoperative nausea and vomiting endpoints and a separate favorable rescue-medication estimate. Trials use different oral preparations and do not measure chronic Parkinson constipation.

fit: nonclinical ginger extract and gastric emptying
assessment: The rat study's abstract reports reversal of a chemically induced delay in stomach emptying. It used an acetone extract and provides no colonic, stool or Parkinson measurement.

fit: healthy volunteer gastric electrical activity after ginger root
assessment: The ginger-root comparison favored healthy stomach electrical patterns under a glucose challenge. The separate misoprostol challenge result remained inconclusive. Gastric electrical frequency is a distinct measurement from emptying or constipation.

fit: aqueous extract in diabetic rats and metabolic endpoints
assessment: The original abstract and earlier IUPS poster share authors, extract regimen and glucose measurements. The publication adds carbohydrate-metabolism measures and provides no stool outcomes. Treat the reports as possibly overlapping.

fit: instant coffee and acute physiology in two healthy subjects
assessment: P4PM-12-16 compares instant coffee with hot water in two healthy people. Facial temperature and heart activity changed, with no measure of patient-rated fatigue.
Grape seed extract affected an isolated vascular response. A companion poster measured distribution after isolated resveratrol. Neither tested dietary grape intake or anxiety.

fit: rat vascular response and constituent distribution
assessment: Grape-derived materials were tested in distinct rat studies. Vascular contraction and constituent distribution differ from Parkinson skeletal rigidity and frozen grape intake.

fit: herb knowledge survey rather than pain response
assessment: The 837-person questionnaire asks about ginger indications and adverse effects. Its percentages report correctness of responses rather than effects following an administered preparation.
